raw.answer: The case asked whether parts of Taiwan's Accountants Act, which set accountants' standards of conduct, duty of care and the range of disciplinary offences, are too vague to be constitutional. The court decided they are not too vague. It found they do not violate the principle of legal clarity or the constitutional protection of the right to work.
raw.held: Article 39, item 6 of the Accountants Act ("other violations of this Act") and Article 17 (no improper conduct, and no violating or neglecting duties in assigned work) do not violate the principle of legal clarity or the right to work protected by Article 15 of the Constitution.

points.text: Professionals facing discipline must be able to foresee which acts or omissions breach their duties and what discipline follows. Abstract terms are allowed if their meaning is not hard to understand, people can foresee them, and courts can review them.

Legislators may use indefinite concepts or catch-all clauses, because they can weigh how complex the facts being regulated are and how well the rule fits individual cases. Legal clarity does not require detailed, specific wording.
Article 39, item 6 covers only duties set by the Accountants Act itself, so its scope can be determined.
Article 17 sets accountants' conduct standards and duty of care. Neglecting duties means failing to do what should be done, or doing work below the standard expected of an accountant.

Accountants' duties cannot be listed exhaustively. Accountants are professionals who passed a state examination, so they can use their expertise to judge which conduct breaches duties and harms clients and public trading security. Discipline is therefore foreseeable.

Some uncertainty remains, but courts can decide individual cases using objective social values and professional ethics. This does not undermine legal certainty, and the rules are necessary to maintain professional standards and public interest, so they do not violate the right to work.

who: Clients and the public relying on accountants

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of the Interior rule was constitutional. The rule said a land expropriation stays valid even if compensation was not paid within 15 days because a legal interpretation was being sought. The court held that the rule does not match the Land Act and conflicts with the constitutional protection of property, so the conflicting part must not be applied.
raw.held: Compensation must be paid within 15 days after the public notice period ends, with limited exceptions, and this deadline must be strictly observed. Article 16 of the Ministry's supplementary rules, to the extent it conflicts with this, must not be applied.

points.text: Expropriation takes property protected by the Constitution through legal procedures. The laws governing it must meet the necessity principle and provide reasonable compensation within a reasonable period.
Owners keep ownership until compensation is paid or properly deposited, but expropriation is a special sacrifice for the public good, so compensation should not be delayed too long.
Article 233 of the Land Act sets payment within 15 days after the notice period ends, and this deadline must be strictly observed, as Interpretation No. 110 said.

The only exceptions are where the owner objected within the notice period and the agency referred the matter for assessment, or where the owner agreed to a delay. Other delays infringe property rights.
Administrative agencies may issue rules to supplement laws, but the content must fit the law's purpose.

Article 16 of the supplementary rules does not fully match the mandatory Article 233 and goes against the constitutional protection of property in Article 15, so it must not be applied to that extent.

raw.answer: The case was about a Ministry of Finance letter saying that, for a tax break on research spending, a "research institution" means one belonging to a government-registered foundation. The court held that the letter does not conflict with the Executive Yuan's rules and does not violate Article 19 of the Constitution. It added that the limits on firms' freedom to choose research partners, and the possible harm to institutions outside the scope, should be reviewed from time to time.
raw.held: The Ministry of Finance's 1986 letter does not conflict with the investment tax credit rules and does not violate Article 19 of the Constitution. The court also said the burdens on firms' choice of research partners and on excluded institutions should be reviewed and improved over time.

points.text: The Investment Encouragement Act's Article 34-1 let the Executive Yuan set the scope of the research spending tax credit, and the Executive Yuan issued the 1985 rules, whose Article 2, item 8 covers commissioning universities or research institutions.
The letter defines research institutions only as those belonging to registered foundations, which speaks only of private legal persons and is not thorough enough.
Article 2 of the rules lists ten kinds of qualifying spending, and spending that fits any of them counts as research and development expense eligible for the credit.
Research institutions outside registered foundations that are commissioned to do research can still apply for case-by-case recognition under item 10 if the cost is truly necessary.
Because of this, producers' tax benefits are not affected, so the letter does not conflict with the rules or with the principle of taxation by law in Article 19.
Even so, firms' freedom to choose whom to commission is limited and excluded institutions may be disadvantaged, so this should be reviewed and improved.

who: Production businesses claiming research tax credits

raw.answer: The case asked what the last part of an earlier ruling (No. 363) meant. That earlier ruling had said that anyone applying to build public facilities while the Investment Encouragement Statute was in force must meet its Article 3. The court explained that this refers to businesses that develop public facilities, and that landowners who are individuals and have not formed a company may invest first but are not automatically entitled to the statute's benefits.
raw.held: The court held that the 'Article 3' requirement in Ruling 363 refers to the item in Article 3, paragraph 1, covering public-facility development businesses. A landowner who is an individual and has not formed a company may invest first under Article 58-1, paragraph 1, but whether they get the various incentives is decided under the statute's own rules. Ruling 363 is supplemented accordingly.

points.text: Ruling 363 had already said that the Taipei market rule requiring applicants to hold all private land in the market site added a restriction the law does not contain, so it was not to be applied.

Where public-facility developers acquire land through purchase talks, mediation or price-based buying, this can harm landowners' protected interests. That is why the amended statute let landowners invest first.

The statute let developers negotiate directly only if the government notified the owner in writing and the owner did not reply within two months or gave up. Compared with the original draft, which had investors negotiate purchases directly, the legislative intent to put landowners ahead of developers is clear.
So the statement in Ruling 363 about meeting Article 3 means that developer businesses applying to build public facilities must meet the requirements in Article 3, paragraph 1, item 11.
A landowner who is an individual and has not formed a company may invest first under Article 58-1, paragraph 1, but whether they get the incentives is handled under the statute's rules.

who: Landowners who are individuals without a company
Applicants to invest in building public facilities

raw.answer: The case asked whether certain provisions of the Military Trial Law are unconstitutional because of how military courts handle trials of soldiers. The court held that, in peacetime, a defendant given a prison term or more by the final military court must be allowed to go directly to the ordinary courts to challenge the judgment as contrary to law. It found several Military Trial Law provisions inconsistent with the Constitution and set a deadline of two years for them to lose effect.
raw.held: Military Trial Law Articles 11, 133 (paragraphs 1 and 3) and 158, and other provisions that bar defendants from going straight to ordinary courts, are inconsistent with the Constitution and lose effect no later than two years after the announcement. The authorities must amend the related laws within that time.

points.text: Personal freedom is protected, and no one may be tried or punished except by a court under legal procedure; people also have the right to bring lawsuits. Active-duty soldiers are people too and share these protections.

The Constitution's exception for active-duty soldiers from the ban on military trial exists because of their special duty to defend the country. It does not give military courts exclusive power over soldiers' crimes or shut out ordinary courts.

Military trial is a form of the state's criminal punishment power, so it must meet minimum due process, including an independent and impartial court and procedure, and must not violate the constitutional principles on the judiciary. Laws limiting soldiers' rights must also respect proportionality.

Because of these protections, peacetime cases ending in a prison term or more in the final military court must allow direct challenge in ordinary courts on the ground that the judgment violates the law.
Article 11 makes the Ministry of National Defense the highest military trial body, so military authorities fully control judicial-type trials, violating separation of powers.
Articles 133 and 158 let military commanders approve or reconsider judgments and approve how trial panels are formed, letting the executive interfere with military trials.

raw.answer: The case asked how far the immunity of Taiwan's legislators for their speech and votes extends under Article 73 of the Constitution. The court said the protection should be defined as broadly as possible and covers speaking, questioning, proposing bills, voting and directly related acts in the legislature. It does not cover acts unrelated to carrying out legislative duties, such as deliberate physical acts that harm others.
raw.held: Legislators are not liable outside the legislature for speech and votes inside it, and this protection covers speeches, questioning, proposals, votes and directly related acts such as party caucus negotiations and public hearings. Acts beyond that scope, such as deliberate physical acts that are not appropriate expression and harm others' legal interests, are not protected, and courts may investigate and try them when necessary.

points.text: The protection exists to safeguard legislators' position and duties and to keep the top legislative body from being disrupted by other state organs.
Legislators need to speak freely and without worry so they can express public opinion, reach majority views and oversee the government, so the protection should be defined as broadly as possible.

Not being responsible outside the legislature means no civil damages or criminal prosecution for duty-related speech and votes, and no administrative liability, though internal discipline for breaking the legislature's own rules is possible, as an earlier interpretation (No. 401) stated.

Because immunity rests on protecting the exercise of legislative duties, acts beyond that scope and unrelated to it, such as deliberate physical acts that are not proper expression and harm others, are not protected.

In individual cases, courts should respect the legislature's self-discipline to the extent needed to keep proceedings running, but may still investigate and try cases to protect social order and victims, for example where the circumstances are serious and clear or the victim files a complaint.

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Civil Servant Discipline Act's rule for when the deadline to seek re-deliberation starts is unconstitutional. The Act sets 30 days from when the related criminal judgment becomes final. The court held that for judgments that cannot be appealed, and for third-instance judgments, the period must instead start from the day the written judgment is served, so that the right to sue under Article 16 of the Constitution is protected.
raw.held: For first- or second-instance judgments that can be appealed, the 30 days run from when the judgment becomes final. For judgments that cannot be appealed and for third-instance judgments, the period runs from the day the written judgment is served. Discipline Committee re-deliberation decision No. 431 and similar cases that conflict with this are no longer to be followed.

points.text: Article 16 of the Constitution protects the right to sue, including fair and prompt trials and effective remedies. Discipline cases affect the right to hold public office, so they require due process and full procedural protection for the person facing discipline.
Re-deliberation exists to fix errors, because a discipline decision becomes final at once and would otherwise have no other remedy. The 30-day limit exists to keep the law stable.

Some judgments become final as soon as they are announced or decided, before the written judgment is served. The disciplined person then can hardly file a request in time, and protection of the right to seek a remedy within the period is clearly insufficient.

So for those judgments the period must start on the day the written judgment is served. The Discipline Committee's No. 431 decision and similar cases did not distinguish whether a judgment could be appealed, and conflict with this, so they are no longer to be followed.

who: Persons seeking re-deliberation of discipline decisions

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the Public Officials Election and Recall Act, which says election lawsuits end after two court levels and cannot be reopened through a retrial, violates the Constitution. The court decided it does not. It said lawmakers are free to set this rule given the nature of election cases, and it does not infringe the right to sue.
raw.held: Article 109 of the Public Officials Election and Recall Act (as amended on July 23, 1994) ends election lawsuits after two instances with no retrial suit. This is within the legislature's freedom to shape the law, does not violate the constitutional right to bring lawsuits, is necessary for the public interest, and does not conflict with Article 23 of the Constitution.

points.text: Article 16 guarantees the right to sue through lawful procedures and a fair trial, but the legislature may reasonably set the number of court levels and procedures according to the nature of the case.
Election and recall disputes mainly protect the public interest, unlike civil suits protecting private rights, although private interests are not wholly ignored.

Officials serve fixed terms, so too many court levels would cause delay, terms could expire before the case ends, and winners could be unsettled in office, harming public business. Quick resolution is therefore needed for legal stability.

A retrial is an extraordinary procedure that corrects factual errors but conflicts with the finality of judgments, so whether to allow it depends on the right and the case type and is for the legislature to decide.
Election and recall cases are party-driven and decided by a panel of judges. Any first-instance oversight can be fixed on appeal, so two hearings can be trusted to reach sound results.
Excluding retrial is therefore necessary for the public interest and does not go beyond what Article 23 allows.

raw.answer: The case asked whether government notices demanding vehicle pollution fines count as appealable administrative decisions, and whether a fine standard that raised fines for people who did not appear within a deadline was constitutional. The court held that such notices can be administrative dispositions that people may challenge, and that the fine standard's deadline-based increases were improper and must lose effect within six months.
raw.held: An agency's one-sided act with legal effect on specific public-law matters is an administrative disposition, even if a notice says it cannot be appealed or further steps follow. The parts of the vehicle pollution fine standard that set minimum fines by appearance time and doubled fines for lateness conflict with this ruling and lose effect at the latest six months after its announcement.

points.text: An administrative disposition is a one-sided act by an agency using public power on a specific public-law matter that has outside legal effect, whatever its wording, form, later steps or no-appeal language.

A notice that directly affects rights and duties and has actually taken effect, such as one stating the fine amount, payment method and doubling for lateness, cannot be treated as a non-disposition just because later steps exist or appeal is barred, since that conflicts with constitutional protection of appeal and litigation rights.
The 1959 Administrative Court precedent only interprets the appeal and administrative litigation rules and does not conflict with the Constitution.
The law sets the fine range and authorizes an agency to set standards within it, meant to let the agency judge by the circumstances of the violation reasonably and avoid arbitrary results.

Article 5 of the fine standard used only appearance time and whether the person appeared to set the minimum fine, not the facts of the violation, so it does not match the authorizing purpose and harms the agency's discretion, even if the upper limit stays within the law.
Doubling fines for not appearing within ten days has no basis in the parent law and no authorization, so it violates the principle of legal reservation, even if meant to encourage voluntary payment.

who: People who receive administrative notices or fine notices
Vehicle owners or drivers fined for pollution
Administrative agencies issuing notices and fines

raw.answer: The case asked whether the National Assembly's speaker and deputy speaker can be paid from the national treasury and whether they can hold other public posts or work. The court said they can be paid a fixed salary, and the legislature's 1997 budget items for them did not conflict with the Constitution. It also said that, unless a law provides otherwise, they may not hold other public offices or carry on a business or profession.
raw.held: The 1997 central government budget items for the speaker's and deputy speaker's allowances and expenses do not conflict with the Constitution. Unless a law says otherwise, the speaker and deputy speaker may not hold other public offices or carry on other work.

points.text: The constitutional amendment created a speaker and deputy speaker, elected by the Assembly's members, starting with the third National Assembly.

The speaker represents the Assembly externally, runs its affairs internally and presides at meetings. This is a regular, ongoing post unlike that of an ordinary delegate, so a fixed salary from the national treasury is allowed.
The items and amounts of pay are within the legislature's power, within reasonable limits.

Earlier interpretations (Nos. 282 and 299) and the delegates' pay law came before the amendment and did not cover pay for the speaker and deputy speaker. So the legislature's approval of the 1997 budget items did not conflict with the Constitution.
When the delegates' pay and expenses law is next amended, it should expressly cover the speaker and deputy speaker as the basis for their pay.

The speaker and deputy speaker are constitutional state organs, hold a regular post and receive regular pay for their status and duties. So unless a law provides otherwise, they may not hold other public offices or carry on a business or profession.

who: National Assembly speaker and deputy speaker

raw.answer: The case asked whether traffic penalty rules punishing pedestrians who cross the roadway in violation of the rules are unconstitutional. The court found the penalty provision in the Road Traffic Management and Penalty Act does not conflict with the Constitution, and that the related safety rule is a valid supplement. It also said the authorities should review and revise that rule on where crossings are placed.
raw.held: Article 78, item 3 of the Act (a fine of NT$120 or 1 to 2 hours of traffic safety lessons for pedestrians who cross the roadway against the rules) is necessary and does not conflict with the Constitution. Article 134, item 1 of the safety rules is a necessary supplement consistent with the Act, but it must be reviewed and revised.

points.text: The state made the Act to manage traffic, keep order and ensure safety, so that vehicles and pedestrians follow the same rules and people's lives, bodies and property are protected.
Penalizing pedestrians who cross the roadway against the rules is necessary for social order and the public interest, so it does not conflict with Article 23 of the Constitution.

The safety rule requiring use of crossings, footbridges or underpasses, and no crossing within 30 meters of them, fills in the penalty's element of 'not following the rules' and fits the Act's purpose.
Crossings, footbridges and underpasses must be placed in suitable locations, considering need, and the convenience and safety of crossing for the public.
The rule review must also consider people with disabilities or limited mobility, and weather or disasters that make these crossings hard to use.
Because Article 78, item 2 of the Act does not penalize pedestrians with proper reason for being unable to use footbridges or underpasses, the rule should be reviewed and revised in that spirit.

who: People with disabilities or limited mobility
Traffic authorities that set up crossings

raw.answer: The case asked whether voters can recall National Assembly delegates and Legislative Yuan members because of improper speech or votes. The court decided they can: the constitutional immunity for speech and votes protects members from criminal, civil and administrative liability, but it does not stop voters in the original electoral district from recalling them.
raw.held: National Assembly delegates and legislators elected from domestic districts may be recalled by voters of their original district on the ground of improper speech or votes, and the immunity provisions (Articles 32 and 73) do not limit this.

points.text: Both bodies are elected representative organs, and the Constitution gives their members immunity for speech and votes so they can speak freely, represent the people and oversee the government without hesitation.

Articles 32 and 73 protect members from civil damages and criminal prosecution for their speech and votes, and from administrative liability apart from discipline under their own internal rules; this is immunity from legal liability toward outsiders.
Recall is a form of citizens' political participation, and Article 133 lets the original electoral district recall an elected person, based on the idea of direct popular rights.

So members are politically accountable to their original voters, who after a period in office may review their conduct, attitude in proceedings and voting positions; no limit on the grounds for proposing recall is needed.
Members elected nationwide at large or by overseas citizens have no original district, so the recall rules do not apply to them.
The 1991 recall law provision (Article 69) matches this: recall by original district voters, not allowed before one year in office, and not applicable to at-large or overseas winners.

who: Voters in their original electoral districts
Members elected at large or by overseas citizens

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Supreme Court precedent (No. 592 of 1964) wrongly limited what counts as an infringement of inheritance rights. The court held that an inheritance right is infringed when someone denies an heir's status and shuts the heir out of the estate. It also held that the precedent, within its stated scope, adds no limit not found in the law and does not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: The precedent does not add restrictions the law does not contain and is not unconstitutional. If heirs did not dispute each other's status at the time of death, and the estate was only interfered with later, that harms rights the heirs already acquired and is not an infringement of inheritance rights under Article 1146 of the Civil Code.

points.text: Inheritance begins on the death of the person who died. Heirs then take over that person's property rights and duties, apart from exceptions in the Civil Code and rights personal to the deceased, without having to declare any intention to inherit.

The Civil Code gives heirs a right to recover an infringed inheritance. An heir need only prove being a true heir, not prove ownership of each item. The right is also time-limited and is distinct from a claim to return a specific object.

Whether inheritance rights are infringed depends on whether someone has denied the heir's status and excluded the heir from possessing, managing or disposing of the estate after the cause of inheritance arose.

Infringement is not limited to people who claimed to be heirs and exercised rights over the estate at the moment inheritance began. It also covers non-heirs falsely claiming to be heirs, or an heir denying other co-heirs' rights, at or after that time.
The claim to recover the inheritance and the claim to return individual objects are separate rights that exist side by side for the true heir.

The precedent only says that a person claiming to be an heir must have infringed the heir's status at the time of death. If heirs did not dispute each other's status then and the estate was interfered with only later, the harm is to rights already acquired. Article 1146 does not apply, and the precedent adds no limit the law lacks.

who: People falsely claiming to be heirs

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Taiwan provincial rule on non-urban land use, which barred approving livestock facilities in water quality and water quantity protection areas where no livestock farm could be newly set up, was unconstitutional. The court decided it was not. It found the rule only carries out other laws and adds no restriction on people's rights that the law does not already contain.
raw.held: The rule (point 25 of the 1995 Taiwan Province non-urban land permitted-use enforcement points) does not conflict with the constitution's protection of property rights (Article 15) or with the legal reservation principle (Article 23).

points.text: The Regional Planning Act aims to conserve land and natural resources, improve living conditions and advance the public interest. Its Article 2 says other laws apply where it is silent, so other laws that fit its purpose, such as the Water Supply Act and the Water Pollution Control Act, apply.
The Interior Ministry's non-urban land use control rules, issued under that Act, say land must be used as permitted, except that where other laws ban or limit a use, those laws govern.
Point 25 carries out the Water Supply Act and the Water Pollution Control Act. It is a specific, clear example under that exception of when a land use may be banned or limited.
The rule is necessary to achieve the Act's purposes and adds no restriction on people's rights that the law does not already contain, so it does not conflict with Articles 15 and 23.
Whether a particular piece of land lies within a protection area is a matter for the courts to decide when they find facts and apply the law.

who: Landowners in water quality or water quantity protection areas

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Finance directive on gift tax for farmland given in several installments was unconstitutional. Under the directive, each earlier gift is taxed first, and once all the farmland has gone to the same eligible heir who keeps farming, the tax is refunded. The court decided the directive is consistent with the laws it implements and does not conflict with Article 19 of the Constitution.
raw.held: The 1994 Ministry of Finance directive on installment gifts of farmland is consistent with the cited laws and does not conflict with Article 19 of the Constitution.

points.text: The gift tax law says farmland of a family farm given to one eligible spouse or heir who can farm and keeps farming is not counted in the gift total.
The agricultural development law likewise exempts family-farm land from estate or gift tax when one heir who can farm takes it and continues farming.
So the exemption requires an heir who can farm and keeps farming, and also that one single heir alone receives the land.
The directive is a necessary instruction from the competent authority to its subordinate offices on how to tax gifts of all the farmland made in installments.
Taxing earlier gifts first and refunding once all the land is with the same recipient meets the legal conditions for exemption.
The directive also fits the agricultural law's purpose of banning the splitting up of farmland and its transfer into co-ownership.

who: Heirs receiving farmland who can farm

raw.answer: Three people were punished under Taiwan's Assembly and Parade Act after holding a street parade without getting a permit, and they asked the court whether the Act's permit system violates the Constitution. The court held that requiring a permit based on time, place and manner is allowed, but struck down the rules that let officials refuse a permit over political views (communism or splitting the country) or vague fears of danger. It also upheld the criminal penalty for ringleaders who ignore dispersal orders, and said the rule giving no room for spontaneous assemblies urgently needs review.
raw.held: The permit system for outdoor assemblies is not unconstitutional as to time, place and manner. Article 11, items 1, 2 and 3 are unconstitutional and lose effect from the announcement date. The criminal penalty in Article 29 is not unconstitutional, while the two-day deadline in Article 9 for spontaneous assemblies conflicts with the Constitution and urgently needs review.

points.text: The court said it could review the permit system as a whole, not only the filing deadline, because the case concerned the requirement of a prior permit and related rules.
Freedom of assembly is part of freedom of expression and is vital to democracy. Limits on it must be clear and necessary.

A permit system based on time, place and manner, which does not look at the purpose or content of the assembly, does not harm freedom of expression. It is not unconstitutional just because it is a prior permit system rather than a notice system.
Refusing a permit for advocating communism or splitting the country lets officials examine political speech in advance, which the court found unconstitutional.

The grounds of danger to national security, public order or public interest, or to life, body, liberty or property, are vague. Refusing a permit on a mere possibility of future harm, with no clear and immediate danger, was found unconstitutional.

The court upheld the rules on restricted zones, who may serve as organizers, clashing applications, unlawful groups and application contents. It also upheld the criminal penalty for ringleaders who keep going after dispersal and stop orders. But the two-day deadline cannot work for spontaneous assemblies, so it urgently needs review.

who: People who hold or take part in outdoor assemblies and parades
Police and other authorities who approve or refuse permits
People holding spontaneous protests after sudden events

raw.answer: The case asked whether a court precedent saying that matters arising from a "special power relationship" cannot be challenged through appeals or lawsuits was constitutional. The court held that a serving military officer whose request to stay on active duty was refused, and who was discharged, may seek relief through administrative appeal and administrative litigation. The part of the precedent that conflicts with this is no longer to be applied.
raw.held: A serving military officer who applied to continue active service, was refused, and was ordered discharged can use administrative appeal and litigation procedures to challenge it. The part of Administrative Court Precedent No. 11 (1959) that conflicts with this must not be applied.

points.text: Article 16 of the Constitution gives people the right to appeal and sue. When rights or legal interests are harmed, that right cannot be limited merely because of someone's status or occupation.

Whether a public official can challenge an administrative action depends on its content. Actions that change an official's status or seriously affect their rights can be taken to the judiciary, as earlier interpretations (Nos. 187, 243, 298 and 338) said.
Soldiers have combat duties and a duty to obey orders, so they cannot be treated the same as civil officials.

Soldiers are still public officials in the broad sense and have a public-law duty relationship with the state. Unless the matter concerns the proper use of military command and discipline powers, their rights should not differ from other officials'.

Refusing an officer's request to stay on active duty and ordering discharge affects whether the officer keeps military status and harms the constitutionally protected right to hold public office. So the officer may use appeal and administrative litigation.

The precedent barred appeals over matters arising from a special power relationship, which conflicts with these principles. The court took up the case despite a 1996 Administrative Court meeting resolution, because the precedent was relied on in the final judgment.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Finance rule on auditing business income tax returns was unconstitutional. The rule says that when a business pays foreign commissions in New Taiwan dollars in Taiwan, up to 3% of the export price is accepted if it has a receipt from the foreign agent. The court held that the rule is not unconstitutional.
raw.held: The court held that the 3% rule for foreign commissions paid in New Taiwan dollars in Taiwan does not conflict with Articles 15, 19 and 23 of the Constitution. It also held that treating these payments differently from other foreign commissions does not violate the equality principle in Article 7.

points.text: The audit rules only cover how business income tax filings are investigated and reviewed, and the provisions on foreign commissions deal with how to prove them and what conditions must be met.

The 3% standard reflects that it is hard to verify whether commissions paid in New Taiwan dollars in Taiwan were actually paid. It draws on the limit that applied under the earlier foreign exchange controls, and the evidence a business must provide depends on whether it goes over that limit.

Amounts above 3% can still be accepted if the business provides other supporting documents, such as the contract, correspondence and proof that the foreign agent received the money, and the tax authority finds them consistent.

The rule only sets technical, detailed matters of recognizing and proving commissions. It simplifies tax collection and prevents inflated foreign commission claims, does not go beyond the income tax law and related rules, and does not increase people's tax burden, so it does not conflict with Articles 15, 19 and 23.
The different treatment only reflects differences in the facts, and because amounts over the standard can still be proven by other documents, it does not violate the equality principle in Article 7.

who: Businesses paying foreign commissions in New Taiwan dollars in Taiwan
Tax authorities auditing business income tax returns
Foreign agents and distributors receiving commissions

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Supreme Court precedent is unconstitutional because it says how a party must state, in a third-instance appeal, that the lower court's judgment violated the law. The precedent requires a specific showing, such as naming the legal provision, principle, interpretation or precedent relied on, or the facts fitting the listed grounds. The court held that the precedent does not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: The Supreme Court precedent (71 Tai-Shang No. 314) only explains how the civil procedure provisions apply and how to specify a legal violation. It adds no restrictions the law does not set, does not impair people's proper exercise of the right to sue, and does not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: The Constitution's right to sue means people can bring suit when their rights are infringed and courts must judge according to law, but the Constitution does not say how the right is exercised, so the legislature may make reasonable rules based on the nature of the case.
The Code of Civil Procedure makes the third instance a review on points of law, so an appeal from a second-instance judgment must rest on a violation of law, and the appeal must state its grounds.

The law requires appeal grounds to be filed, and an appeal that does not file them is dismissed without a request to fix it. This lets the third-instance court review the case and prevents abusive appeals.
The Code does not say how appeal grounds must be written, and the precedent fills that gap by explaining the text of the law and how to specify a legal violation.
Because the precedent adds no restrictions the law does not provide and does not impair the proper exercise of the right to sue, it does not conflict with the Constitution.

who: Litigants claiming a lower-court judgment violated the law

raw.answer: The case asked whether the air pollution control fee rules, and the items they charged, were unconstitutional. The court held that the fee is a "special public levy" (特別公課), not a tax, and that the law authorizing the rules was specific enough, so the rules do not violate the Constitution. However, it said that charging only on fuel, and not on pollutants from fixed sources, breaches fair sharing of the burden and must be fixed promptly.
raw.held: The fee collection rules, including charging mobile pollution sources by the amount of fuel used, were held not to violate the Constitution. Charging only fuel since 1 July 1995 and not other pollutants from fixed sources violates the principle of fair sharing of public charges, and the agencies should promptly fix this.

points.text: The Constitution requires the state to protect the living environment, and air pollution control is an important part of that duty. The fee follows the polluter-pays principle and pays into a fund for improving air quality.
The fee is a special public levy, not a tax. Its purpose, targets and use must be set by law, but the law may authorize rules if the authorization is specific and clear.
Judged against the whole Air Pollution Control Act, Article 10 is not lacking in specificity regarding purpose, targets, places and use.

The fee rates and categories were listed in the budget of the air pollution control fund and passed by the Legislative Yuan, so the legal basis and main items rest on law and budget. Still, the agencies should improve how rates and spending fit local needs and regulate them by law, and must use the money consistently with its purpose.

The Act covers mobile sources such as vehicles, and Article 10 does not exclude them. Charging by fuel used is reasonable because emissions are closely tied to fuel use, and it takes technology and cost into account.

Collecting only on fuel and not on other pollutants from fixed sources breaches fair sharing of the burden and may give the public the false impression that the fee is for revenue. The agencies should improve this quickly, including by building a periodic inspection system for mobile sources.

who: Owners and users of vehicles that use fuel

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Department of Health ruling (a 1982 letter of interpretation) was unconstitutional when it said that practitioners of traditional Chinese medicine treating patients with Western drugs falls outside their scope of work. The court held that the letter does not conflict with the constitution's protection of the right to work. It reasoned that Chinese medicine practitioners are expected to treat by traditional Chinese methods, and that keeping medical specialties distinct serves the public interest.
raw.held: The Department of Health's 1982 letter, which treats a Chinese medicine practitioner's use of doctor-directed Western drug preparations as improper conduct and use of over-the-counter Western drugs as outside their scope of work, is not in conflict with the constitution's protection of the right to work.

points.text: The constitution protects the right to work, but the law may reasonably limit how people work and what qualifications they need when the public interest requires it.

The law divides doctors into physicians, Chinese medicine practitioners and dentists so each gives specialized care, protects patients and promotes public health; the rule that a clinic's responsible doctor supervise staff to follow their own professional rules also serves the public interest.
Chinese medicine practitioners should treat by traditional Chinese methods, which is what patients trust them to do.

A person who holds both physician and Chinese medicine qualifications may combine both methods, because that is within their professional scope. Apart from this case, a Chinese medicine practitioner prescribing doctor-directed Western drugs or over-the-counter Western drugs goes against the principle of professional classification and patient trust, even if they are also a pharmacist.

Where a Western drug is 'for use only on a doctor's instruction', 'doctor' does not include Chinese medicine practitioners, and prescribing over-the-counter Western drugs is not using their traditional skill.
The letter merely explains the scope of a Chinese medicine practitioner's work and fits the purpose of the medical practitioner and medical care laws, so it does not conflict with the right to work.

raw.answer: The case asked whether an Administrative Court meeting resolution was unconstitutional. The resolution said a company whose real business is mainly large-scale securities trading is not "not specialized in securities trading", even if its registered business items do not include it. The court decided the resolution is consistent with Article 27 of the Statute for Encouraging Investment and does not violate the principle of taxation by law in Article 19 of the Constitution.
raw.held: The Administrative Court's October 14, 1992 resolution is consistent with Article 27 of the Statute for Encouraging Investment and does not conflict with the constitutional principle of taxation by law (Article 19). Such companies fall outside the suspension of securities transaction income tax.

points.text: The Statute aimed to encourage investment through tax breaks, and set conditions so benefits are shared fairly and tax avoidance to get improper breaks is prevented.
Laws on tax matters should be read in line with taxation by law, using the law's purpose, economic meaning and the fairness of substantive taxation.
A company running business outside its registered scope, or failing to register it, still actually carries on that business; the Company Act consequences do not change that fact.
So whether a business is "not specialized in securities trading" must be determined from its actual operations, not its registration.
A company that actually does huge securities trading, with trading income far above its registered business income, is mainly in that business and cannot use registration gaps to claim the exemption.
Part of the Statute's Enforcement Rules, Article 32, that does not fully match the legislative purpose should not be applied.

who: Companies whose registered business omits securities trading

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the Road Traffic Management Penalty Act that bars a second appeal (再抗告) against court rulings on traffic penalties violates the constitutional right to bring a lawsuit. The court decided that the procedure does not conflict with that right. It reasoned that the procedure gives people a chance to defend themselves and present evidence before a judge.
raw.held: Article 87 of the Road Traffic Management Penalty Act lets a person object to a penalty in the local court and appeal that ruling once, but not a second time. The court held this does not conflict with the right to bring a lawsuit under Article 16 of the Constitution.

points.text: The right to sue means people can ask a court for relief when their rights are harmed, and courts must judge according to law. Protection must be real and effective, not just formal.

Whether such disputes go to ordinary courts or administrative courts, and which procedure applies, is for the legislature to decide, weighing the nature of the right, the type of case, and the functions of existing court systems.

Traffic penalties such as fines and suspension of licenses are punitive administrative actions. Under Article 87, objections go to the traffic division of an ordinary court rather than through the usual administrative appeal and administrative litigation route.
The legislature designed this based on the nature of the affected interests, how often such cases occur, the urgency of final decisions, and the workload of the bodies hearing them.

The procedure gives parties the chance to defend themselves and submit evidence, and a judge under Article 80 of the Constitution weighs the evidence and decides fairly, so it meets due process and does not conflict with Article 16.

raw.answer: The case asked whether it was unconstitutional that the Enforcement Act of the Civil Code Family Book made no special rule when the rules on spouses' combined property were amended. The court held that the Act's general rule (Article 1) is constitutional, but that leaving property that already existed before the 1985 amendment under the old rules, with the husband keeping the rights, fails to carry out the constitutional guarantee of equality between men and women. It told the relevant authorities to review and amend the Act promptly.
raw.held: Article 1 of the Enforcement Act does not conflict with the Constitution. However, because the Act made no special rule for the amended Civil Code Article 1017, combined property that arose before the amendment still goes by the old rules, which does not achieve gender equality, and the authorities must promptly review and amend the Act. The estate and gift tax provision on a decedent's spouse applies to husband or wife alike and is not unconstitutional.

points.text: Article 1 of the Enforcement Act respects legal orders that existed before the Family Book took effect or before an amendment, to protect legal stability, and allows special rules where an old order should not continue. So it does not conflict with the Constitution.

The old Article 1017 gave ownership of much of the combined property, and the income from the wife's original property, to the husband. Because of the Constitution's Article 7 on equality of men and women, it was amended in 1985, and the earlier Supreme Court precedent is no longer followed.

The Enforcement Act set no special rule for the Article 1017 amendment, so combined property that arose before the amendment and still exists remains under the old rules, with the husband continuing to hold the rights. This fails to carry out the equality guarantee.

The old rules also left the husband with ownership of the income from the wife's original property and with management of the combined property. The authorities should promptly revise the Act to balance this against preserving the existing legal order.
The tax provision exempting a decedent's spouse's original or special property from the estate total covers husband and wife alike, so it does not violate Article 7.
Differences in the estate total caused by applying the old Article 1017 result from the latter part of Article 1 of the Enforcement Act, so the tax provision itself cannot be called unconstitutional.

who: Married couples whose combined property arose before the 1985 amendment
Wives whose property is still under the old rules
Heirs and estates affected by the tax provision
Authorities responsible for amending the Enforcement Act

raw.answer: The case asked whether an Executive Yuan order and an Interior Ministry letter were unconstitutional for using a fixed sum to estimate a tenant farmer's living costs. The court found that this method was unrealistic and unreasonable and conflicted with the Constitution's protection of farmers. It ruled that the order and letter should no longer be applied.
raw.held: The Executive Yuan order and the Interior Ministry letter, which applied a fixed-amount minimum living cost standard to work out a tenant's family living expenses, do not fit the Constitution's aim of protecting farmers and may no longer be applied.

points.text: The Constitution protects the right to live and requires the state to protect farmers and improve their livelihood.

The Land Rent Reduction Act's rule barring a landlord from taking back land when the tenant would lose the family's livelihood aims to protect tenant farmers from serious harm to their family life and survival.
The order and letter used a fixed, unchanging sum from a military service classification table to estimate the tenant's living costs.
This method ignored price differences between regions and each farm family's actual income, spending and hardship, such as medical and insurance costs.
So the method is not close to reality, is unreasonable, and conflicts with the Constitution's protection of farmers.

who: Landlords seeking to take back leased land
Farm families dependent on rented land

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of the Interior circular was unconstitutional. The circular said that even when a main urban plan had been in force over two years, a building permit could be refused if the plan required a detailed plan first. The court held that this went beyond what the Urban Planning Act allows and conflicts with the constitutional protection of property, so it must not be applied.
raw.held: The Ministry of the Interior's 1984 circular, and the matching condition in the Miaoli County plan notice on issuing building permits, exceeds the law and conflicts with the constitutional protection of property rights, so it should not be applied.

points.text: The 'other matters to be stated' clause in the main plan covers only matters similar in nature to the items before it. It cannot be used to restrict or contradict matters the law already expressly provides for.

Restricting building and land alteration in areas without a detailed plan serves the public interest. But property rights cannot be left in limbo because the authority delayed issuing a detailed plan beyond two years.

So the proviso lets building authorities designate building lines and issue permits once the main plan has been published for over two years and a building line can be fixed or main public facilities are built. This lifts the building restriction and protects people's right to use their property.
A main plan therefore cannot require that a detailed plan be completed before a permit is issued, because that would block the proviso from applying.

The Ministry's circular and the Miaoli County notice condition on permits go beyond the Act and add a restriction the proviso does not contain. They conflict with property protection and should not be applied.

who: Local governments such as Miaoli County

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule implementing the Soldiers' Land Grant Certificate Handling Act was unconstitutional in how it defines "officers without posts" (無職軍官). The Act mentions such officers in Article 10 but does not define them. The court held that the implementing rule's definition is a supplementary rule that fits the Act's purpose and does not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: Article 3, item 16 of the Act's implementing rules, which defines an officer without a post, supplements the Act, does not go against its legislative purpose, and does not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: The Act was made to take back land grant certificates already issued and to pay compensation at different rates. Article 10 treats certain discharged officers without posts as if they had already received certificates, to protect their rights.
The Act does not define "officer without a post", but its purpose points to the Executive Yuan's 1959 measures for handling officers without military posts.

Those measures list the kinds of people covered, limit them to people living in government-controlled areas up to 30 June 1958, and treat those who skipped the registration survey as discharged and not handled later.
The registration period ran from 8 June to 18 October 1959. The measures were repealed in 1964 once that period ended.

So the implementing rule, which requires registration on file by 18 October 1959, a discharge order, and confirmation of status by the Ministry of National Defense, is a supplementary rule needed to carry out the Act. It does not go against the Act's purpose or the Constitution.

who: Former officers without posts who left their units in Taiwan
People claiming compensation under the Soldiers' Land Grant Certificate Handling Act
Officers who registered with the Ministry of National Defense by 18 October 1959

raw.answer: The case asked whether two Executive Yuan letters were unconstitutional because they let the government keep using old roads on private land (roads the public has long used) without buying the land. The court held that when such a road meets certain conditions, the owner has made a special sacrifice and the state must pay fair compensation. The parts of the two letters that conflict with this can no longer be relied on.
raw.held: The state must lawfully expropriate land under such roads and compensate owners, and if money is short it must set a deadline and pay over time or by other means. The parts of the two Executive Yuan letters that conflict with this are no longer to be applied.

points.text: The constitution protects property rights, so the state may take private property for public benefit only with fair compensation.
A road gets a public-use easement only if public passage is truly necessary, the owner did not stop the public at the start, and the use has lasted so long that no one remembers its beginning.
Once those conditions are met, the owner can no longer freely use the land, which is a special sacrifice for the public good, so the authorities should expropriate and compensate.
If funds are short, governments must set a workable deadline to raise money and pay year by year, or make up the loss in other ways such as installment bonds, user fees, tax offsets or public land.
Where all private land along a road is expropriated, continuing to use an easement road without compensation by order alone violates the equality principle.
If a road loses its original function because of changed geography or social conditions, it should be reviewed and abolished.

who: Owners of private land under long-used roads
Members of the public using such roads

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the Customs Anti-Smuggling Act could be valid when it made customs refuse to hear an objection unless the person paid half the fine or tax as a deposit, or gave equal security, within 14 days. The court decided the rule unnecessarily cuts off people's right to appeal and sue, so it conflicts with Article 16 of the Constitution.
raw.held: Article 49 of the Customs Anti-Smuggling Act, which rejects objections when the deposit or security is not provided in time, conflicts with Article 16 of the Constitution and may no longer be applied. The relevant part of Interpretation No. 211 is changed.

points.text: Article 16 of the Constitution protects the right to petition for administrative review and to sue, which lets people seek relief when public power harms their rights and lets agencies correct wrongful decisions. Under Article 23, this right may be limited by law only when necessary.

The court has consistently held that requiring payment of all or part of a tax or fine, or security, as a condition for challenging a penalty is an unnecessary restriction when it strips those who cannot pay of legal remedies.
The rule does have a purpose: it lets customs handle each case and prevents people from objecting just to delay or avoid enforcement.
However, customs may already ask a court to seize or freeze property without providing security after the decision is served, so enforcement of the original decision is already secured.

The law also has no way for a person to ask for temporary exemption from paying or providing security, so those unable to pay would lose any chance of administrative remedy. The restriction is therefore clearly unnecessary and conflicts with Article 16.

who: People who object to customs penalties
People unable to pay the deposit or provide security

raw.answer: The case asked whether the "monthly salary amount" used to work out severance pay for political appointees (政務官) includes cash payments beyond basic salary. The court decided that it does: the base includes the monthly salary and also other cash benefits.
raw.held: The "monthly salary amount" used as the base for calculating political appointees' severance pay must include "other cash benefits" as well as the monthly salary.

points.text: Under the current law, severance pay for political appointees is calculated from the "monthly salary amount," and their monthly pay consists of a monthly salary and an allowance (公費).

The law does not clearly say whether the monthly salary amount for appointees' severance means salary plus allowance, so it must be read as a whole in light of the purpose of the civil servant retirement and pension rules in force when the severance law was amended.

Ordinary civil servants' lump-sum retirement pay was based on the final monthly salary amount, and appointees' pensions followed the civil servant pension rules, so appointees' severance and pension standards should match the old civil servant standards.
The old civil servant retirement law defined "monthly salary amount" as actual basic salary plus other cash benefits, so it differs from basic salary alone and includes other cash benefits.

The court noted that the law does not separate appointees who serve according to politics or policy from those with guaranteed terms; whether this conflicts with the constitution is outside this ruling, so the current law is applied until it is amended.
The amount of severance owed for the other cash benefits must follow the calculation standard set by law at the time of retirement from office.

who: Civil servants under the old retirement and pension rules

raw.answer: The case asked which court should hear disputes when a government agency sells or leases public property. The court decided that these disputes are private-law contract matters, so they go to the ordinary (civil) courts rather than the administrative courts.
raw.held: When an administrative agency sells or leases public property on behalf of the national treasury, it is acting through a private-law contract, not an administrative disposition. Disputes about it are to be resolved through civil court procedures, and the two administrative court precedents saying so do not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: The Constitution gives the Judicial Yuan authority over civil, administrative and disciplinary cases, which shows civil and administrative trials are distinct.
The right to sue is protected, but which court hears and conducts a case is for law to set, as an earlier interpretation (No. 297) said.
Current law uses a dual court system: public-law disputes go to administrative courts and private-law disputes go to ordinary courts.

An agency selling or leasing public property for the national treasury is not using public power to produce a one-sided legal effect, so it is not an administrative disposition but a private-law contract act.
So parties who dispute such a sale or lease must use civil litigation.
The two administrative court precedents (1969 No. 270 and 1972 No. 159) fit the legal division of jurisdiction, do not harm the right to sue, and do not violate the Constitution.

who: People disputing government sales or leases of public property
Administrative agencies selling or leasing public property

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Taipei City road-management rule was unconstitutional because it let authorities bury underground facilities beneath existing or planned roads without buying the land or paying compensation for the underground use. The court held that the rule, to the extent it provides neither purchase nor compensation for that underground use, conflicts with the constitutional protection of property and may no longer be applied.
raw.held: The part of Article 15 of the Taipei City Urban Road Management Rules that allows underground use of such road land with neither purchase nor compensation is inconsistent with the ruling's principles and should no longer be applied. Acquisition of such land must follow Interpretation No. 400 and Article 48 of the Urban Planning Act.

points.text: Property rights are protected by Article 15 of the Constitution. When state action causes a loss beyond what people should bear as their social responsibility, creating a special sacrifice, the state must pay reasonable compensation.

Owners of existing roads that carry a public easement can no longer freely use their land. This is a special sacrifice for the public good, so the state must acquire it with compensation, or set a time limit and gradually fund it or compensate by other means, as Interpretation No. 400 stated.

Laws already exist for acquiring or buying reserved land under urban plans, and owners may apply to build underground parking or shops before their land is expropriated, to preserve their use and benefit of it.

Before acquiring such land, authorities may use it for underground facilities such as power lines, water pipes and sewers. They must follow the proportionality principle, choosing the place and method causing the least loss, and give fair compensation for the owner's loss.
The Taipei rule neither buys the land nor provides compensation for underground use, so it does not fit these principles and is no longer to be applied.

raw.answer: Several lawmakers asked Taiwan's Constitutional Court whether the Vice President may also serve as Premier (head of the Executive Yuan), whether a Premier must resign when a new President takes office, and whether a Legislative Yuan resolution urging the President to renominate a Premier binds him. The court said the two jobs are not clearly incompatible, but holding both does not fit the constitution's design, so the situation should be handled appropriately. It also said the Premier's resignation for a new President is a courtesy that the President may handle at his discretion, and that the Legislative Yuan's resolution exceeded its powers and does not bind the President.
raw.held: Holding both offices is not clearly forbidden but does not fully match the constitution's intent of separate people in the posts, and the facts behind the case should be handled accordingly. A Premier's courtesy resignation is not a constitutional duty, and the President's handling of it is not for the court to review. The Legislative Yuan's resolution exceeded its powers, is only a suggestion, and has no binding force on the President.

points.text: The question is a legal one about whether two constitutional posts can be held together, not a purely political one, so the court decided it on the merits.

Having the Vice President serve as Premier has not become a binding constitutional custom, because precedents were contested, including one case of immediate resignation, and the constitutionality of the practice is disputed.
The constitution does not forbid the dual role, and it does not violate separation of powers.
The Vice President has no specific constitutional powers beyond succeeding or acting for the President, so there is no division of powers, checks or conflict of interest with the Premier.

The Vice President and President are not legally one unit, and the succession problems of holding both posts have ways of being handled, so the dual role is not clearly unconstitutional. But if the President leaves office or cannot act, one person would hold several posts, which does not fit the intended succession design of separate people.
A Premier's resignation when a new President takes office is a courtesy, not a constitutional duty. How the President responds is a discretionary act of state that the court does not review.

The Legislative Yuan has no power to resolve that the President must act, and such a resolution would create a no-confidence system the constitution does not adopt, so its resolution is merely advisory.

who: The Legislative Yuan and its members

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Finance letter of 1977 was unconstitutional. The letter said that when companies merge, the surviving company cannot deduct the losses of the company that was absorbed. The court held that the letter matches the income tax law and does not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: The Ministry of Finance letter (6 September 1977, 台財稅字第35995號) is consistent with the income tax law and not unconstitutional. After a merger, profit and loss are calculated afresh from the merger date, and earlier losses of the merging companies cannot be deducted. Whether mergers should get tax benefits is a matter for the legislature.

points.text: Business income is calculated from the current year's revenue minus costs, expenses, losses and taxes. Losses from earlier years generally cannot be counted in the current year, under Articles 24(1) and 39 (first part) of the Income Tax Act.
The proviso to Article 39 lets companies with complete books and timely filing deduct earlier losses, in order to encourage honest tax filing.

This loss deduction applies only if the company has profit this year and no merger happened in the deduction period. If companies merge, profit and loss are calculated afresh from the merger date and cannot be traced back to the pre-merger companies' losses.
The letter says the surviving company and the company that disappeared in the merger are not the same company, so the surviving company cannot deduct the absorbed company's losses.
The letter fits the legislative purpose, does not breach the principle that taxes must rest on statute, and does not conflict with the Constitution.
Whether mergers should receive tax benefits is a legislative question.

raw.answer: The case was about whether a 1994 amendment to the Educational Personnel Employment Act could let school staff who never passed the required civil service exams be transferred between schools. The court decided that the 'may be transferred among schools' wording conflicts with the Constitution. That wording stops having effect from the day the ruling was announced.
raw.held: The words 'and may be transferred among schools' in Article 21, paragraph 2 of the July 1, 1994 version of the Educational Personnel Employment Act conflict with Constitution Articles 85 and 7 and the earlier Interpretation No. 278, and lose effect from the date of this ruling.

points.text: Constitution Article 85 requires public servants to be chosen by open, competitive exams and not appointed unless they pass, so school staff must qualify through the relevant exams.

Interpretations of the Constitution by the Grand Justices bind all state bodies and the people, and the legislature, though it has wide freedom, may not go beyond the Constitution or those interpretations.

Staff hired by selection before the Act took effect did not gain the same qualification as exam passers under Interpretation No. 278; their earlier rights are protected only as far as they do not conflict with the exam principle, so they may stay only at their original school.
Hiring by selection before the Act was an exception made while the legal system was incomplete, and it should not be widened by legislation, to avoid breaching equality.
Allowing transfers among schools makes the legal position of non-exam staff almost the same as that of qualified staff, which is unfair to those who passed exams.
For the inconvenience of staying at one school, the court suggested the Examination Yuan hold exams to settle their qualifications.

who: School staff hired without passing exams
School staff who passed the exams

raw.answer: The case asked whether a government measure, the Regulations on Handling Exit of Males of Draft Age, could lawfully restrict draft-age men from leaving the country. The court held that restricting exit is a major limit on freedom of residence and movement, and that no statute allowed it or clearly authorized it by regulation. So the measure's exit restriction conflicts with the Constitution and will lose effect.
raw.held: Article 8 of the Regulations on Handling Exit of Males of Draft Age, which limits exit by draft-age men, is inconsistent with the Constitution because it lacks legal authorization. It loses effect from the date of the ruling, at the latest when six months have passed.

points.text: Article 10 of the Constitution protects the freedom to live where one chooses and to move or travel freely. Limiting it must meet Article 23's necessity standard and be set by law or by a regulation clearly authorized by the legislature.

How much a matter must be set by statute rather than regulation depends on what is regulated and how heavily rights are limited. Limits on other freedoms must be set by law, and any authorization to issue regulations must be specific and clear. Only minor, technical details of carrying out a law may be left to regulation.
Article 20 of the Constitution, on the duty to serve in the military according to law, means important matters about military service must be set by law or by a regulation clearly authorized by law.

The Military Service Act and its Enforcement Act contain no provision restricting exit by draft-age men, and the Enforcement Act's Article 45 only authorizes the Executive Yuan to make conscription rules. Nothing clearly authorizes such an exit restriction, or lets the Executive Yuan delegate it to the Ministry of the Interior.
Although the exit restriction aims to stop men from leaving to evade military service, it is a major limit on people's freedom and so conflicts with the constitutional principles above.

who: Executive Yuan and Ministry of the Interior

raw.answer: The case asked whether drug advertising rules requiring prior government approval violate the Constitution. The court held that the approval requirement in the Pharmaceutical Affairs Act, Article 66, paragraph 1, and the related rule on prize or reward promotions in the Enforcement Rules, Article 47, item 2, are consistent with the Constitution. It also said the authorities should keep reviewing the scope of the approval requirement.
raw.held: Requiring drug sellers to get approval from the health authority before running drug ads is consistent with Articles 11 and 15 of the Constitution. The rule letting authorities delete or refuse ads using prize or reward promotions that may encourage drug abuse stays within its parent law and does not conflict with the Constitution.

points.text: Drug advertising is an economic activity for gain and a form of commercial expression, so it is protected by the Constitution. Commercial speech that does not shape public opinion, find truth or express belief is not protected equally with other speech.
Because drug ads bear heavily on public health, they can be regulated more strictly to protect the public interest.

Prior approval aims to keep drug ads truthful and protect health. It puts the review in one authority, which can examine the drug's function, the ad's content and market impact through a professional, objective process, so it is necessary for the public interest.

The rule on prize or reward promotions rests on the authorization in Article 105 of the Act and implements Article 66. It fits the legislative purpose, does not exceed the parent law and adds no restriction on people's rights that the law lacks.

Ads provide information and society has a major interest in free flow of commercial information, so the authority should weigh the necessity of the approval requirement's matters, content and scope and revise it from time to time under the proportionality principle.

raw.answer: A person challenged a 1992 Government Information Office letter that set out standards for deciding whether a publication is obscene under the Publication Act. The Constitutional Court held that the letter does not conflict with the Constitution. It also stressed that judges are not bound by such letters and that the standards must be reviewed as social views change.
raw.held: The 1992 Government Information Office letter, an illustrative interpretation with specific conditions, does not conflict with the Constitution. Obscenity is defined in objective terms, authorities must keep reviewing their interpretations, and judges decide individual cases independently without being bound by the letter.

points.text: The court accepted the case because a final court judgment relied on the letter to establish facts, and the applicant specifically argued it was unconstitutional. Judges are independent and not bound by administrative interpretations.
Freedom of publication is protected by the Constitution, but publishers must act responsibly, and the state may restrict publications that harm public morals or order by law.

Agencies may issue necessary interpretations of abstract legal concepts. Obscene publications are those that objectively stimulate or satisfy sexual desire, cause ordinary people shame or disgust, and harm sexual moral feelings and social morals. They are told apart from artistic, medical or educational works by looking at the whole work and its purpose, using society's general views at the time.

The letter is an illustrative interpretation with specific conditions, such as inducing sexual desire, stressing erotic acts, deliberately exposing the body or over-describing sex. Merely printing text or pictures does not qualify. It adds no restriction the law does not provide, so it does not conflict with the Constitution.
Ideas of public morals change with society, so the agency must keep reviewing its interpretations. It must respect free expression while protecting good customs and young people's well-being.

Administrative penalties and criminal punishment have different elements and can find facts separately, so judges decide whether a work is obscene on their own judgment. The ruling covers only this letter, not other matters under the Publication Act.

who: Government Information Office and other authorities

raw.answer: The case asked whether postal rules limiting compensation for registered mail are unconstitutional. In particular, compensation covers lost or stolen registered mail but not damaged ordinary registered mail. The court decided the Postal Law and the postal regulations at issue do not conflict with the Constitution, though it asked the postal authority to review how special types of mail are handled.
raw.held: The Postal Law's limit on compensation for registered mail (lost or stolen, but not damaged) and Postal Regulations Articles 227 and 228 are not unconstitutional. The competent authority should review whether special types of mail need their own rules.

points.text: The state runs public utilities like the post to provide affordable, steady service. It may limit their compensation or damages liability, but such limits affect people's rights and must meet Article 23 of the Constitution.
The Postal Law does provide compensation for some damage, such as damaged registered parcels, insured-value mail and declared-value mail, so it does not ignore damage altogether.

Ordinary registered mail is mostly documents or letters sealed by the sender, and their value is hard to determine objectively. Excluding damage compensation for them weighs fees, service nature, costs and harm, is needed to keep the postal service running, and stays within the legislature's freedom and the proportionality principle, so it does not violate property rights.
Special mail such as stamp collections has no objective way to value damage and invites disputes, so the authority should review its handling, fees, storage and compensation rules.

Regulation Articles 227 and 228 only set the conditions for compensation liability: responsibility ends on proper delivery, and no later claim is allowed if the recipient signed for the mail without objecting. They stay within the Postal Law's delegation and add no new limits.
These rules match the Universal Postal Convention's approach, which Taiwan is not a party to but which serves as a general international norm.

who: The postal service and its authority
Senders of special mail such as stamp collections

raw.answer: The case asked whether a court precedent was unconstitutional for denying withholding-at-source tax treatment to overseas Chinese and foreign investors whose spouse lived in Taiwan. The Constitutional Court held the precedent added a spouse-residence condition that the statute does not contain, which violates the constitutional principle that taxes must be based on law. The precedent therefore must not be applied.
raw.held: The 1974 Administrative Court precedent (No. 673) added a condition, that no spouse lives in Taiwan, that the law does not contain. It violates the principle of taxation by statute and must not be applied.

points.text: The investment incentive laws were meant to encourage production businesses and speed economic growth, and withholding tax at a set rate was meant to ease investors' tax burden and attract overseas Chinese and foreign investment.
Because those laws are special laws relative to the Income Tax Act, people who benefit from the investment incentives should get the tax-reducing rules in them.

The Constitution's Article 19 means people owe tax only under what the law sets, such as who pays, tax items, rates, methods and reductions. Precedents cannot add rules the law lacks or increase the tax burden.

The incentive law's article 17 refers only to individuals not residing in Taiwan and sets no condition about a spouse's residence. Those who meet its terms get withholding at the set rate rather than year-end filing under the Income Tax Act.
The precedent added a no-spouse-in-Taiwan condition, which adds a limit the law does not have, so it conflicts with taxation by statute.

The Court did not decide whether a person or spouse actually counts as non-resident because of a home or other facts, which is a question of fact and law application. It also did not address the Civil Code equality complaint, which was not specifically argued.

who: Overseas Chinese investors approved to invest in Taiwan
Foreign investors approved to invest in Taiwan
Investors who are company directors, supervisors or managers
Investors whose spouse lives in Taiwan
