raw.answer: The case asked whether the Civil Service Insurance Act is unconstitutional for not letting insured people get their premiums back, and for giving old-age benefits only to people who retire under the law. The court said that having no premium refund is constitutional. But it said that giving old-age benefits only to retirees, and saying nothing about other people who leave service, conflicts with the constitutional protection of property rights and should be reviewed and amended promptly.
raw.held: Not providing for return of premiums once paid does not conflict with the Constitution. However, Article 16, paragraph 1 of the Act, which gives old-age benefit rights only to those who retire under the law and says nothing about other people who leave service, is inconsistent with the property rights protection in Article 15 of the Constitution and should be reviewed and amended promptly.

points.text: Civil service insurance is a state social welfare system using insurance principles, and covers paid staff in legally established agencies and public officials, who must all join.
Premiums are shared by the insured and the government and form the financial base for benefits. They are also used to share risk among the group's members.

Once paid, premiums are used in the insurance operation and serve as the fund for benefits, so the insured cannot ask for them back unless otherwise provided. Having no refund rule is therefore constitutional.
Part of the premiums must be set aside as an old-age benefit reserve under the approved reserve rules.

The principal and interest of this reserve resemble an accumulation of deposits by all the insured and are not the insurer's assets. So a person who has paid for the required years and then leaves service has a right to claim a benefit.

Giving the old-age benefit claim only to those who retire under the law, and saying nothing about other leavers, conflicts with Article 15's protection of property rights. The conditions and amount of any claim are for the legislature.

who: Insured civil servants and public officials
Insured people who leave service without retiring

raw.answer: The case asked whether rules made by the Ministry of Economic Affairs and six other agencies unconstitutionally limited civil engineers. The rules say civil engineers may handle building structure work only for buildings up to 36 meters high. The court held that this limit does not conflict with the constitution's protection of the right to work.
raw.held: The 36-meter limit on civil engineers' building structure work does not conflict with the constitutional protection of the right to work. Civil engineers who qualified after 19 September 1978 remain properly subject to it.

points.text: The constitution protects the right to work, but for the public interest the law may regulate how people work and what qualifications they need. Laws cannot cover every detail, so they may authorize agencies to divide the scope of each profession's practice by order.

The agencies set the 36-meter limit under the Technicians Act article 12(2) to divide civil engineers' scope from structural engineers'. Civil engineers' scope includes building structure work but is simpler and narrower than structural engineers' scope.

Civil and structural engineering both affect public safety. Having specialists do their own specialized work serves the public interest and is necessary, so it does not conflict with the right to work.

The 1978 rules had let practicing civil or architect engineers handle building structures until enough structural engineers were available. This was a temporary measure for social needs at that time, and it was abolished on 2 October 1987.

The later rules exempt those who qualified as civil engineers by 18 September 1978 and had designed buildings of 36 meters or more by 2 October 1987. Those who qualified from 19 September 1978 onward remain subject to the limit.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule written by the Examination Yuan was unconstitutional. The rule limited the application of the regulations on ranking reserve military personnel who move into public service to those who transferred on or after January 16, 1987. The court held the rule was not unconstitutional.
raw.held: Article 10, paragraph 5 of the implementing rules limits their scope to people who transferred on or after January 16, 1987 (the 76th year of the Republic). This does not go beyond what the statute authorized and does not violate the constitutional guarantee of equal protection of the right to work.

points.text: The equality principle in Article 7 of the Constitution protects substantive equality, so the law may treat people differently based on differences in the facts and the purpose of the legislation.
A law may authorize an administrative agency to issue implementing rules that make reasonable and necessary provisions about factual differences the law itself sets out.

The earlier rules, from 1980, on the ranks and pay scales of officers and noncommissioned officers moving into civil service responded to real differences in military service years, so they were necessary provisions.

In 1988 the Examination Yuan limited the rules to transfers on or after January 16, 1987, because the Civil Service Appointment Act and the Civil Service Pay Act had been newly written in 1986 and took effect on that date.

The limit was meant to fit the new laws and to take account of different circumstances, so it did not go beyond the authorization in the statute and does not conflict with equal protection of the right to work.

who: Reserve military personnel moving into public service
Civil servants appointed under the new laws

raw.answer: The case asked whether two broad provisions in Taiwan's Land Act and Urban Planning Act, which list the purposes and uses for which the government may expropriate private land, violate the Constitution. The court held that they do not conflict with the constitutional protection of property rights. It also said that the Land Act's wording is not specific enough and that the expropriation procedures are incomplete, so the authorities should review and revise them.
raw.held: Land Act Article 208, item 9 and Urban Planning Act Article 48 are not in conflict with the Constitution's protection of property rights. The relevant authorities should review and amend the vague wording of Land Act Article 208 and the incomplete expropriation procedures.

points.text: The Constitution protects property, but the state may limit land ownership or take land for public needs as provided by law. Paying fair compensation is one means of meeting those needs.
The Constitution does not set the conditions and procedures for expropriation but leaves them to legislation.

The two provisions are broad statements of purpose and use. They do not allow expropriation at will, because other Land Act provisions and the least-loss principle in Article 49 of the Land Act Enforcement Act still limit it.
The Land Act sets mandatory procedures for carrying out expropriation. Original owners can reclaim land that is not used as planned or approved after compensation is paid.
The provisions mean that expropriation may only serve public-interest or public-utility undertakings that are necessary, so they do not conflict with property protection.

Because expropriation seriously affects property rights, the law should spell out its conditions and procedures in detail, including clear purposes, public-interest standards and urgency. Owners and other interested parties should be heard before a plan is finalized, and the vague wording and incomplete procedures should be revised.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of the Interior rule is unconstitutional. The rule bars people who occupy farmland from applying to register a superficies right (地上權, a right to use another person's land for buildings, structures or bamboo/trees) acquired through long-term occupation. The court decided the rule does not conflict with the constitution's protection of property rights.
raw.held: The rule that people occupying farmland (耕地) may not apply to register a superficies right acquired through long-term occupation does not conflict with the constitutional protection of people's property rights.

points.text: Under Civil Code Article 832, a superficies right is a right to use another's land for buildings, other structures, or bamboo or trees, so the land must be suited to those uses. This also applies when someone claims the right through long-term occupation.
Planting bamboo, as the ruling reads it, does not include cultivating plants on land by human effort for regular harvest.
Under Land Act Article 82, land designated for one type of use may not be used for another purpose.
Farmland is defined by Article 3, item 11 of the Agricultural Development Act, and it is used only for cultivation.

Because farmland is unsuited to buildings, structures, or bamboo and trees for forestry, it does not meet the requirements for a superficies right, and no such right can be registered through long-term occupation.

So the Ministry of the Interior's 1988 rule, item 2 of point 3 of its review guidelines, which bars occupiers of farmland from applying, does not conflict with the constitutional protection of property.

raw.answer: The case asked whether the training rules for the senior and junior civil service exams were unconstitutional because they did not exempt people who already held a similar civil service job from practical training. The court decided the rules do not conflict with the Constitution, because training is part of the legal exam process and cannot be credited away unless a law says so. It added that the responsible agency should consider whether people with closely matching, qualified experience should always be denied credit.
raw.held: The rule that provides no exemption from practical training is consistent with the Constitution. Training is a legal part of the exam process and, unless a law provides otherwise, cannot be offset by credit.

points.text: Under the Civil Service Examination Act, people who pass the written exam must complete training and pass it before the exam process is complete.
Because training is a legal part of the exam process, it cannot be credited away unless a law says otherwise.
The training has two stages: basic training, which can be waived for some people, and practical training, which builds the skills needed for the work.
Practical training serves a special purpose and does not necessarily depend on a person's earlier public service experience or years of service, so having no credit rule is not a conflict.
The rule applies equally to everyone who passes the senior or junior exam, so it does not conflict with Articles 7 and 18 of the Constitution.
The court said the responsible agency should review whether people with a qualified, matching position and similar work should never get credit for real experience.

who: People who pass the senior or junior civil service exams
Current or former civil servants who take these exams
The agency responsible for exam training

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Finance rule letting it punish insurance agents, brokers and notaries (warnings, suspension, or revoking their licenses) was constitutional. The court decided that the rule goes beyond what the Insurance Act authorized and is inconsistent with the constitutional protection of people's rights. The rule will lose effect within one year of the ruling.
raw.held: Article 48, paragraph 1, item 11 of the Insurance Agent, Broker and Notary Management Rules, which allows punitive administrative actions, is inconsistent with the constitution's protection of rights. It loses effect no later than one year after the ruling is announced.

points.text: Punitive administrative actions for breaking administrative duties limit people's rights, so the conditions and consequences must be set by law. A law may authorize orders to fill in details only if the purpose, scope and content of the authorization are specific and clear.
Even under a general authorization, an order may only cover detailed and technical matters. It may not go beyond the law and create punishment provisions on its own.

Article 177 of the Insurance Act lets the Ministry of Finance make management rules and regulate these professionals' conduct as needed. But it does not clearly set out the conditions or consequences of punishment for breaching duties, apart from penalties already stated in Article 167-1.

The rule allows warnings, suspension for one month to three years, or license revocation. These are punitive actions that restrict rights, even though made in view of public interest, so they needed a law or a clearly authorized order as their basis.
Because the rule went beyond the law's authorization and set punishment conditions and consequences itself, it conflicts with the constitution's protection of rights.

Considering the need for the rule and the time needed to amend the law, the court gave one year before it lapses. Other punitive provisions in the rules that limit rights should also be reviewed and amended quickly.

raw.answer: The case was about whether a tax rule could limit the income tax exemption for supported relatives to those registered at the same household address as the taxpayer. The court decided that the rule went beyond the law and conflicts with the constitutional principle that taxes must be set by statute. Whether a relative counts as a family member depends on actually living together, not only on household registration.
raw.held: The implementing rule requiring the same household registration as a condition for the exemption restricts the scope of the parent law and violates Article 19 of the Constitution. The part that conflicts with this interpretation may no longer be applied.

points.text: Article 19 means the key elements of a tax, such as who pays, what is taxed, the tax base and the rate, must be set by statute. Implementing rules may only address matters related to carrying out the law and cannot add to or reduce tax obligations or their conditions.

The exemption exists to encourage taxpayers to meet their legal duty to support certain relatives or family members. If implementing rules could freely change its conditions, that would conflict with the principle that taxes are set by statute.

The income tax law grants the exemption for other relatives or family members only if they are actually supported by the taxpayer and meet the Civil Code conditions, which means a head-of-family and family-member relationship.
Under the Civil Code, a household is defined by living together with the aim of permanent shared life, not necessarily by being registered at one address.
People who live together permanently as a family are sometimes not registered together. Police officers, whose registration must be at their place of service, are given as an example.

The implementing rule made same household registration the only test, so taxpayers could not prove that a supported person really lived with them as family. This narrowed the parent law and violated Article 19.

who: Taxpayers claiming exemptions for supported relatives
Relatives or family members supported by taxpayers
People whose household registration differs from where they live
Tax authorities applying the implementing rule

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Civil Servant Discipline Act is unconstitutional in how it sets out disciplinary punishments and the length of removal and suspension periods. The court held that the provisions are not unconstitutional, because discipline differs from criminal punishment and the legislature has wider freedom to shape it. However, it noted that the Act sets no upper limit on the periods of barred reappointment after removal or of suspension, and said the relevant authorities should review and amend this.
raw.held: Articles 2 and 9 of the Act, which set only general rules on which misconduct gets which discipline, and Articles 11 and 12, on removal and suspension periods, do not violate the Constitution. The lack of a maximum for the barred-reappointment period and the suspension period affects civil servants' rights and should be reviewed and amended by the relevant authorities.

points.text: Discipline rests on the public-law duty relationship between the state and civil servants, so it is not quite the same as criminal punishment and does not need the same strict specificity as criminal law.
Because of this difference, the legislature has broader freedom to shape the elements and consequences of discipline.
General wording in Articles 2 and 9 is acceptable because civil servants' breaches vary widely in type and seriousness, and the law cannot list them all in advance.
Leaving out maximum periods in Articles 11 and 12 is meant to let the disciplinary body choose a fitting measure in each case.
Article 10 requires the disciplinary body to weigh all circumstances, such as motive, purpose, means and resulting harm, so the discipline fits the breach.
Even so, having no upper limit on the barred-reappointment and suspension periods affects civil servants' rights and should be reviewed and amended to better protect them.

raw.answer: The case asked whether it is unconstitutional for a court to let a debtor who applies to pause a compulsory enforcement do so by setting a security (a deposit) in the court's order. The court decided that this rule does not conflict with Article 7 of the Constitution. It said the security protects the creditor and does not add to the debtor's burden.
raw.held: The rule in Article 18, paragraph 2 of the Compulsory Enforcement Act, letting a court set adequate and reliable security when it orders enforcement stopped at the debtor's request, does not conflict with Article 7 of the Constitution.

points.text: Enforcement must rest on an enforcement title. Once it begins, it does not stop unless the law says otherwise, and it continues until the title is carried out.
In certain situations, such as the debtor seeking restoration, a retrial, or an objection suit, the law lets the court order a stop. This avoids harm to the debtor from continued enforcement.
The security ensures the creditor can be compensated for losses if the debtor's request to stop enforcement was improper. This balances the interests of both sides.
The security does not guarantee that the debtor's original debt will be paid, so it adds no extra burden on the debtor.

A creditor applies for enforcement on an enforcement title, while a debtor asks for a stop on grounds that justify one and is ordered to give security. The underlying facts differ, so it is hard to say this violates Article 7.
